blocks.text: In 1985 the musician Clive Wearing developed herpes simplex encephalitis. Afterwards he could not form new memories and lived in a perpetual present, greeting his wife with joy each time she entered as if they had not met for years. Yet he could still sit at a piano and play and conduct complex music fluently. One brain, two kinds of memory: one destroyed, one untouched.

blocks.markdown:
**Memory** is the encoding, storage and retrieval of information. Memory is divided by duration and by type. **Working (short-term) memory** holds a small amount of information for seconds to minutes, relying heavily on prefrontal cortex. **Long-term memory** is divided into two main systems:

- **Declarative (explicit) memory**: facts and events that can be consciously recalled and 'declared'. It includes **episodic** memory (personal events, for example what you ate this morning) and **semantic** memory (facts, such as the capital of France). It depends on the **medial temporal lobe** (hippocampus and adjacent entorhinal and parahippocampal cortices) and the **diencephalon**.
- **Non-declarative (implicit) memory**: skills and habits expressed through performance, without conscious recall. **Procedural memory** (motor skills such as riding a bicycle or playing an instrument) depends on the **basal ganglia (striatum)** and **cerebellum** with the motor cortex. Priming and simple conditioning are also implicit; emotional conditioning depends on the **amygdala**.

rows: Hippocampus, medial temporal lobe, diencephalon, neocortex
Can be learned in a single exposure

blocks.title: Classifying memories
blocks.prompt: Classify each: (a) remembering that Paris is the capital of France; (b) remembering the route you walked to work this morning; (c) tying shoelaces without thinking; and name the key brain structures.

steps.text: (a) is a fact detached from the occasion of learning: semantic, declarative memory, depending on the medial temporal lobe and neocortex.
(b) is a personally experienced event with time and place: episodic, declarative, depending on the hippocampus.
(c) is an automatic motor skill performed without conscious recall: procedural, non-declarative, depending on the striatum and cerebellum.

blocks.answer: (a) semantic; (b) episodic; (c) procedural. Only the first two are declarative.

blocks.markdown:
**The hippocampus and consolidation.** The hippocampus is not the long-term store for memories, but it is needed to **consolidate** new declarative memories: to turn a labile, recently acquired trace into a stable long-term memory distributed in the neocortex. In **systems consolidation** the hippocampus binds together the cortical areas representing the different elements of an experience, and over weeks to years the cortical connections strengthen so the memory becomes less hippocampus-dependent.

The classic hippocampal pathway is the **trisynaptic circuit**: the **entorhinal cortex** projects via the **perforant path** to the **dentate gyrus**; mossy fibres link the dentate to **CA3**; the **Schaffer collaterals** link CA3 to **CA1**; and CA1 projects to the subiculum and back to the entorhinal cortex. The hippocampus connects to the mammillary bodies by the **fornix**, then to the anterior thalamus and cingulate gyrus (the **Papez circuit**).

Bilateral hippocampal damage causes **anterograde amnesia**: inability to form new declarative memories, with preserved working memory, intact procedural learning and preserved remote memories. **Retrograde amnesia** is loss of memories formed before the injury. Recent memories are lost more than remote ones (a temporal gradient), because older memories have already been consolidated in the cortex. **Korsakoff syndrome** (thiamine deficiency, often in chronic alcohol use) damages the mammillary bodies and thalamus and produces severe anterograde amnesia with confabulation.

blocks.title: What amnesia spares
blocks.text: Hippocampal amnesia spares immediate recall, procedural skills and old memories. This dissociation is the evidence that declarative and procedural memory use different systems.

blocks.title: Predicting what a patient can still do
blocks.prompt: A 55-year-old man has bilateral hippocampal destruction. Over several days he practises a mirror-drawing task. Each day he insists he has never seen the task, yet his accuracy improves. Explain.

steps.text: He cannot form new declarative memories, because hippocampal consolidation is lost, so he denies having seen the task.
Mirror drawing is a procedural skill dependent on the striatum, cerebellum and cortex, which are intact.
Procedural learning therefore proceeds without conscious recall.

blocks.answer: Preserved procedural (implicit) memory with lost declarative (explicit) memory.

blocks.markdown:
**Long-term potentiation (LTP)** is a long-lasting increase in synaptic strength after brief, high-frequency stimulation, and is the leading cellular model of learning. It was first described in the hippocampus, and is best understood at the **CA3-CA1 (Schaffer collateral)** synapse. The postsynaptic membrane contains two glutamate receptors: **AMPA receptors** (permeable to $\text{Na}^+$), which carry the basic fast EPSP, and **NMDA receptors**, which at the resting potential are blocked by $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ sitting in the pore. The NMDA receptor opens only when **glutamate is bound and the postsynaptic cell is depolarised** (relieving the Mg$^{2+}$ block): it is a **coincidence detector**. Then $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ enters, activates kinases such as CaMKII, and leads to phosphorylation and insertion of more AMPA receptors, increasing the response to the same glutamate release. Later phases need new protein synthesis and structural change.

LTP is a good learning model because it is **rapid, long lasting, input-specific** (only the active synapses strengthen) and **associative** (weak input paired with strong input potentiates), as predicted by Hebb's idea that cells that fire together wire together.

blocks.caption: Size of LTP, comparing the EPSP slope or amplitude after induction with its baseline.

blocks.title: LTP is a model, not memory itself
blocks.text: LTP shows how synapses can store information, but it is evidence for a mechanism, not a direct measure of memory. Blocking NMDA receptors in the hippocampus impairs both LTP and some forms of new learning in animals, which supports the link.

points: Declarative (episodic and semantic) memory depends on the medial temporal lobe and hippocampus; procedural memory depends on the striatum and cerebellum.
The hippocampus consolidates new declarative memories, which are eventually stored in the neocortex; bilateral damage produces anterograde amnesia with preserved procedural learning.
LTP at hippocampal synapses depends on NMDA receptors, which require glutamate and postsynaptic depolarisation, allow Ca2+ entry, and increase AMPA receptor function, strengthening the synapse.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of declarative (explicit) memory?

options.text: Typing without looking at the keys

distractorRationale.b: Correct: recalling a personal event is episodic, declarative memory.

questions.explanation: Declarative memory consists of consciously recalled facts and events. Recalling a personal event is episodic memory, whereas skills and conditioned responses are expressed without conscious recall.

questions.stem: A violinist with extensive hippocampal damage can still play a piece she learned years ago and can improve on a new piece with practice. Which brain structures best underlie this preserved ability?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: procedural memory is supported by these structures.
distractorRationale.c: These are part of the Papez circuit, relevant to declarative memory.

questions.explanation: Playing an instrument is procedural memory. It depends on the basal ganglia, cerebellum and motor cortex, none of which is damaged by hippocampal lesions.

questions.stem: True or false: a patient with bilateral hippocampal damage can learn a new motor skill even though he cannot remember practising it.
questions.explanation: Procedural learning depends on the striatum and cerebellum rather than the hippocampus, so it is preserved. The patient cannot form new declarative memory of the practice sessions.

questions.stem: After bilateral medial temporal lobe resection, a patient can repeat a seven-digit number immediately and recalls his childhood home, but cannot recall a conversation held ten minutes earlier. Which term best describes this pattern?

distractorRationale.a: Retrograde amnesia is loss of pre-injury memories; his are largely intact.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: inability to form new declarative memories, with intact immediate recall and old memories.

questions.explanation: He retains working memory and remote memories but cannot consolidate new episodes, which is the hallmark of anterograde amnesia after hippocampal damage.

questions.stem: According to the systems consolidation model, what is the role of the hippocampus in memory?

options.text: It is the permanent store of all remote memories
It binds new experiences and helps consolidate them into stable memories distributed in the neocortex

questions.correctOptionText: It binds new experiences and helps consolidate them into stable memories distributed in the neocortex

distractorRationale.a: Remote memories are largely spared in hippocampal damage, so it is not the sole permanent store.
distractorRationale.c: Procedural skills depend on the striatum and cerebellum.
distractorRationale.d: Working memory depends largely on the prefrontal cortex.

questions.explanation: The hippocampus links the cortical elements of an experience and gradually strengthens their connections, so the memory becomes independent of it. This explains why recent memories are lost before remote ones.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with long-standing alcohol dependence and poor nutrition develops profound inability to form new memories and fills the gaps with plausible invented stories. Which structures are characteristically damaged?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Korsakoff syndrome damages these diencephalic structures of the Papez circuit.
distractorRationale.b: Visual cortex damage causes visual loss.
distractorRationale.c: Vermis damage causes gait ataxia, not amnesia.
distractorRationale.d: The substantia nigra is involved in Parkinson disease.

questions.explanation: Thiamine deficiency damages the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus, which are linked to the hippocampus in the Papez circuit. The resulting anterograde amnesia with confabulation is Korsakoff syndrome.

questions.stem: At a CA3-CA1 synapse, which condition is required to open the NMDA receptor channel so that LTP can be induced?

options.text: Glutamate binding together with postsynaptic depolarisation that relieves the Mg2+ block
GABA binding together with Ca2+ entry

questions.correctOptionText: Glutamate binding together with postsynaptic depolarisation that relieves the Mg2+ block

distractorRationale.a: At resting potential Mg2+ still blocks the pore.
distractorRationale.b: Hyperpolarisation would reinforce the Mg2+ block.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the NMDA receptor is a coincidence detector.
distractorRationale.d: GABA is inhibitory and not required.

questions.explanation: The NMDA receptor opens only when glutamate is bound and the postsynaptic membrane is depolarised enough to expel Mg2+. Only then does Ca2+ enter and trigger the changes of LTP.

questions.stem: Before tetanic stimulation the slope of a hippocampal field EPSP is 0.80 mV/ms. One hour afterwards, the slope is 1.40 mV/ms. By what percentage has the synapse been potentiated?
questions.explanation: Potentiation = (1.40 - 0.80) / 0.80 x 100 = 0.60 / 0.80 x 100 = 75%. A sustained increase of this kind after brief high-frequency stimulation is the defining feature of long-term potentiation.

questions.stem: Explain how long-term potentiation is induced at the CA3-CA1 synapse, and state two properties that make it an attractive cellular model of learning.
markingGuide: High-frequency presynaptic stimulation releases glutamate, which acts on AMPA and NMDA receptors
AMPA receptors depolarise the postsynaptic cell, relieving the Mg2+ block of NMDA receptors
NMDA receptors open when glutamate is bound and the cell is depolarised, allowing Ca2+ entry
Ca2+ activates kinases (for example CaMKII), leading to insertion and phosphorylation of AMPA receptors, so the synapse responds more strongly
Properties: persistence, input-specificity and associativity (coincidence detection, Hebbian)
questions.explanation: LTP is a Hebbian process driven by coincident presynaptic glutamate release and postsynaptic depolarisation, which opens NMDA receptors and raises postsynaptic Ca2+. The resulting increase in AMPA receptor function is long lasting and specific to the active synapses, as one would expect of a memory trace.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman has bilateral damage to the hippocampi after hypoxia. Contrast what she can and cannot do in terms of declarative and procedural memory, and explain the role of the hippocampus.
markingGuide: She cannot form new declarative (episodic and semantic) memories: anterograde amnesia
Remote memories and working memory are largely preserved
Procedural learning and skills remain intact (striatum, cerebellum)
The hippocampus consolidates new declarative memories into long-term cortical stores
Example of preserved skill or lost recall is given
questions.explanation: Without the hippocampus new experiences cannot be consolidated, so she cannot recall recent events, but systems for skills and old memories are intact. This dissociation shows that declarative and procedural memory rely on different structures.
